items.title: $APLD: What Changed in Today’s November Investor presentation from $APLD $APLD’s November investor presentation shows more signed business,
items.content_excerpt: $APLD: What Changed in Today’s November Investor presentation from $APLD $APLD’s November investor presentation shows more signed business, stronger lease economics, construction progress and clearer campus locations. This comparison uses the June 2026 corporate deck, the latest earlier full presentation I could verify. Against June, $APLD’s signed capacity increased 10.6% to 1,560 MW; base-term lease value rises 15.1%, from $35.73 billion to $41.13 billion; and value including all renewals reaches $98.36 billion from $85.66 billion. The new 150 MW lease supplies the $5.4 billion increase. The $98.36 billion includes base terms and assumes all renewals occur. The $41.13 billion represents expected rent over 15 to 18 years, subject to delivery and contractual conditions; neither figure is today’s asset value. Clearer locations for Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 2 June left the locations of PF3 and DF2 undisclosed. No more. November’s campus table now identifies Polaris Forge 3 in Center, North Dakota, and Delta Forge 2 in Alabama. ￼I know that location is in Brookwood. These are the existing 300 MW PF3 project and 210 MW DF2 project, respectively. The presentation gives shareholders a more concrete picture of the $APLD portfolio across North Dakota, Louisiana and Alabama. For PF3, naming Center, ND as the location helps connect the campus with the Base Electron generation project described in $APLD’s October 10-Q. Naming Alabama gives investors a clearer jurisdiction for following DF2’s power and permitting developments, although its city remains unspecified in the deck. But that city is Brookwood. The new lease deserves a closer look The new lease agreement covers 150 MW for 18 years, with three five-year renewal options. It carries $5.4 billion of expected base rent, approximately $12.7 billion with all renewals, an expected 85% site NOI margin and planned deliveries during 2028. The location of this separate 150 MW lease remains undisclosed. Dividing $5.4 billion by 18 years produces $300 million of average annual rent, or $2 million per MW. PF3 and DF1 each produce approximately $1.67 million per MW using the same calculation. That puts the new contract about 20% higher on average annual rent per MW, consistent with $APLD management’s statement that pricing improved. Its larger value reflects both a longer term and better average economics. This calculation does not establish a 20% increase in starting rent because the escalation schedules and project differences are not disclosed. At the assumed 85% margin, the new lease contributes approximately $255 million of average annual site NOI. Against projected construction costs of $11 million to $13 million per MW, that equals roughly 13.1% to 15.5% of development cost annually before financing and corporate costs. The Enlarged $2.30 billion NOI figure is useful, with a specific meaning The June investor presentation described approximately $2 billion of average annualized NOI. The November presentation provides a site-by-site model totaling approximately $2.30 billion, with a $2.22 billion to $2.38 billion range. The model divides each lease’s base-term value by its duration, applies the expected operating margin and assumes all capacity operates and bills for a full year. The strongest execution evidence In the November Investor Presentation is the operating capacity $APLD’s operating AI capacity rises from 100 MW in June to 275 MW in the updated deck. $APLD’s November 24 announcement explains the latest milestone: PF1 has 250 MW operational, and PF2’s first 25 MW data hall achieved Ready for Service on schedule. Base-build commissioning also finished for the first 75 MW at PF2, with the remaining 50 MW still requiring fit-out and customer delivery. $APLD achieving ready for service at a second campus provides evidence that $APLD can repeat its construction and commissioning process. That is execution. However, only about 18% of the 1,560 MW signed portfolio is online. The November presentation identifies another 1,285 MW under construction, with contracted deliveries extending through 2028. PF2’s additional 100 MW remains unsigned. It belongs in potential expansion, not contracted backlog. The precise signed figure is 1.56 GW; 1.66 GW includes that proposed expansion. Customer quality and the delivery schedule Approximately 75% of base-term lease revenue comes from investment-grade counterparties, versus approximately 70% in June. Although the presentation does not identify those investment-grade tenants, they are $ORCL for Polaris Forge 2 and $META for Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 1 and 2. Better tenant credit can support financing and reduce collection risk. This describes the tenants’ credit quality, not a rating of every $APLD loan. The deck shows PF1 and PF2 completing their contracted deliveries in the first half of 2027, PF3 extending through the second half of 2028, DF1 from mid-2027 through the first half of 2028, DF2 in the first half of 2028, and the new lease during 2028. November presents a 3.5 GW to 4 GW goal by 2030, an increase from the approximately 3 GW by 2031 states in the prior investor presentation. $APLD managment assumes roughly 450 MW to 600 MW of annual additions per year and explicitly labels this a goal, not guidance. Of course, if they can pull this off, the gain in market cap should be very large The chart’s 1.66 GW starting point includes contracted development and the unsigned expansion. It states that operating capacity is 275 MW. Utility-power pipeline figures also differ from critical IT capacity, which excludes cooling and other facility power. Financing remains central to shareholder returns The Macquarie example illustrates approximately 80% project debt, $2.25 million per MW of preferred capital and $0 to $0.35 million per MW of $APLD common-equity funding. $APLD retains 85% of the common interest in the illustrated structure. This can support substantial construction with limited upfront common funding, but the preferred capital initially carries a 12.75% dividend and other return protections. PIK dividends preserve cash today while increasing the preferred claim. Separately, the November 23 announcement confirms a $300 million delayed-draw bridge for DF1 at SOFR plus 300 basis points (6.91% interest), with a 364-day maturity. Draws depend on conditions, including regulatory approvals, and completion requires additional financing. It supports construction progress BUT the entire campus is not fully funded yet. Management expects remaining project financing for DF1 and PF3 in first-quarter 2027 and DF2 in second-quarter 2027. To me, $APLD getting competitive interest rates on these 3 AI factories are critical to the company’s success or failure. $CHRN and Base Electron add further opportunities The $CHRN section now highlights a planned roughly 50 MW $MSFT deployment and a frontier-lab partnership (either Anthropic or Oosn AI) with up to $7.5 billion of total contract value. These carry separate financing, delivery and acceptance requirements. November describes $APLD as the majority owner. June specified approximately 97%. The current percentage needs verification before assigning per-share value. $CHRN’s contract value should not be added to $APLD real-estate lease backlog as though the two have identical economics. For Base Electron, the updated deck adds the October power-purchase agreement and associated conditions. $APLD owns approximately 10%, giving its shareholders an indirect interest. The generation facility still needs development and financing, and Base Electron may terminate the PPA if financial close does not occur by March 31, 2027. The Bakken East Pipeline’s 2029-2030 schedule is relevant to later expansion, not proof of power availability for every 2028 delivery. The most persuasive improvements are the additional signed rent, stronger average pricing on the new lease and delivery at a second AI campus. The presentation also provides a clearer way to model the contracted portfolio. Existing site margins and construction-cost assumptions remain unchanged. Of course, the key to shareholder value (besides a good macro) is completing construction, securing the remaining financing and converting property income into cash attributable to common shareholders. In all I thought this was a solid investor presentation showing strong execution and a massive expected pipeline. Sources: November presentation: https://ir.applieddigital.com/_assets/_6036fbbfdc67ef4d6a0fd28f08b1ac6a/appliedblockchaininc/db/2905/27279/pdf/APLD_Presentation_11232026.pdf June presentation: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1144879/000149315226027984/ex99-2.htm New lease and financing outlook: https://ir.applieddigital.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/165/applied-digital-secures-new-150-mw-18-year-lease-with PF2 Ready for Service: https://ir.applieddigital.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/166/applied-digital-achieves-initial-25-mw-ready-for-service-in ￼ DF1 bridge: https://ir.applieddigital.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/164/applied-digital-announces-300-million-senior-secured October 10-Q: https://ir.applieddigital.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0001144879-26-000059/apld-20260831.htm

items.title: $APLD: What Changed in Today’s November Investor presentation from $APLD $APLD’s November investor presentation shows more signed business,
items.content_excerpt: $APLD: What Changed in Today’s November Investor presentation from $APLD $APLD’s November investor presentation shows more signed business, stronger lease economics, construction progress and clearer campus locations. This comparison uses the June 2026 corporate deck, the latest earlier full presentation I could verify. Against June, $APLD’s signed capacity increased 10.6% to 1,560 MW; base-term lease value rises 15.1%, from $35.73 billion to $41.13 billion; and value including all renewals reaches $98.36 billion from $85.66 billion. The new 150 MW lease supplies the $5.4 billion increase. The $98.36 billion includes base terms and assumes all renewals occur. The $41.13 billion represents expected rent over 15 to 18 years, subject to delivery and contractual conditions; neither figure is today’s asset value. Clearer locations for Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 2 June left the locations of PF3 and DF2 undisclosed. No more. November’s campus table now identifies Polaris Forge 3 in Center, North Dakota, and Delta Forge 2 in Alabama. ￼I know that location is in Brookwood. These are the existing 300 MW PF3 project and 210 MW DF2 project, respectively. The presentation gives shareholders a more concrete picture of the $APLD portfolio across North Dakota, Louisiana and Alabama. For PF3, naming Center, ND as the location helps connect the campus with the Base Electron generation project described in $APLD’s October 10-Q. Naming Alabama gives investors a clearer jurisdiction for following DF2’s power and permitting developments, although its city remains unspecified in the deck. But that city is Brookwood. The new lease deserves a closer look The new lease agreement covers 150 MW for 18 years, with three five-year renewal options. It carries $5.4 billion of expected base rent, approximately $12.7 billion with all renewals, an expected 85% site NOI margin and planned deliveries during 2028. The location of this separate 150 MW lease remains undisclosed. Dividing $5.4 billion by 18 years produces $300 million of average annual rent, or $2 million per MW. PF3 and DF1 each produce approximately $1.67 million per MW using the same calculation. That puts the new contract about 20% higher on average annual rent per MW, consistent with $APLD management’s statement that pricing improved. Its larger value reflects both a longer term and better average economics. This calculation does not establish a 20% increase in starting rent because the escalation schedules and project differences are not disclosed. At the assumed 85% margin, the new lease contributes approximately $255 million of average annual site NOI. Against projected construction costs of $11 million to $13 million per MW, that equals roughly 13.1% to 15.5% of development cost annually before financing and corporate costs. The Enlarged $2.30 billion NOI figure is useful, with a specific meaning The June investor presentation described approximately $2 billion of average annualized NOI. The November presentation provides a site-by-site model totaling approximately $2.30 billion, with a $2.22 billion to $2.38 billion range. The model divides each lease’s base-term value by its duration, applies the expected operating margin and assumes all capacity operates and bills for a full year. The strongest execution evidence In the November Investor Presentation is the operating capacity $APLD’s operating AI capacity rises from 100 MW in June to 275 MW in the updated deck. $APLD’s November 24 announcement explains the latest milestone: PF1 has 250 MW operational, and PF2’s first 25 MW data hall achieved Ready for Service on schedule. Base-build commissioning also finished for the first 75 MW at PF2, with the remaining 50 MW still requiring fit-out and customer delivery. $APLD achieving ready for service at a second campus provides evidence that $APLD can repeat its construction and commissioning process. That is execution. However, only about 18% of the 1,560 MW signed portfolio is online. The November presentation identifies another 1,285 MW under construction, with contracted deliveries extending through 2028. PF2’s additional 100 MW remains unsigned. It belongs in potential expansion, not contracted backlog. The precise signed figure is 1.56 GW; 1.66 GW includes that proposed expansion. Customer quality and the delivery schedule Approximately 75% of base-term lease revenue comes from investment-grade counterparties, versus approximately 70% in June. Although the presentation does not identify those investment-grade tenants, they are $ORCL for Polaris Forge 2 and $META for Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 1 and 2. Better tenant credit can support financing and reduce collection risk. This describes the tenants’ credit quality, not a rating of every $APLD loan. The deck shows PF1 and PF2 completing their contracted deliveries in the first half of 2027, PF3 extending through the second half of 2028, DF1 from mid-2027 through the first half of 2028, DF2 in the first half of 2028, and the new lease during 2028. November presents a 3.5 GW to 4 GW goal by 2030, an increase from the approximately 3 GW by 2031 states in the prior investor presentation. $APLD managment assumes roughly 450 MW to 600 MW of annual additions per year and explicitly labels this a goal, not guidance. Of course, if they can pull this off, the gain in market cap should be very large The chart’s 1.66 GW starting point includes contracted development and the unsigned expansion. It states that operating capacity is 275 MW. Utility-power pipeline figures also differ from critical IT capacity, which excludes cooling and other facility power. Financing remains central to shareholder returns The Macquarie example illustrates approximately 80% project debt, $2.25 million per MW of preferred capital and $0 to $0.35 million per MW of $APLD common-equity funding. $APLD retains 85% of the common interest in the illustrated structure. This can support substantial construction with limited upfront common funding, but the preferred capital initially carries a 12.75% dividend and other return protections. PIK dividends preserve cash today while increasing the preferred claim. Separately, the November 23 announcement confirms a $300 million delayed-draw bridge for DF1 at SOFR plus 300 basis points (6.91% interest), with a 364-day maturity. Draws depend on conditions, including regulatory approvals, and completion requires additional financing. It supports construction progress BUT the entire campus is not fully funded yet. Management expects remaining project financing for DF1 and PF3 in first-quarter 2027 and DF2 in second-quarter 2027. To me, $APLD getting competitive interest rates on these 3 AI factories are critical to the company’s success or failure. $CHRN and Base Electron add further opportunities The $CHRN section now highlights a planned roughly 50 MW $MSFT deployment and a frontier-lab partnership (either Anthropic or Oosn AI) with up to $7.5 billion of total contract value. These carry separate financing, delivery and acceptance requirements. November describes $APLD as the majority owner. June specified approximately 97%. The current percentage needs verification before assigning per-share value. $CHRN’s contract value should not be added to $APLD real-estate lease backlog as though the two have identical economics. For Base Electron, the updated deck adds the October power-purchase agreement and associated conditions. $APLD owns approximately 10%, giving its shareholders an indirect interest. The generation facility still needs development and financing, and Base Electron may terminate the PPA if financial close does not occur by March 31, 2027. The Bakken East Pipeline’s 2029-2030 schedule is relevant to later expansion, not proof of power availability for every 2028 delivery. The most persuasive improvements are the additional signed rent, stronger average pricing on the new lease and delivery at a second AI campus. The presentation also provides a clearer way to model the contracted portfolio. Existing site margins and construction-cost assumptions remain unchanged. Of course, the key to shareholder value (besides a good macro) is completing construction, securing the remaining financing and converting property income into cash attributable to common shareholders. In all I thought this was a solid investor presentation showing strong execution and a massive expected pipeline. items.content_excerpt: Michael Burry, known for predicting the 2008 housing market collapse, has sold the remaining half of his bearish Nasdaq 100 put position, saying his portfolio is now temporarily almost entirely bullish amid increased market volatility. Burry told subscribers he exited the position Wednesday as technology stocks came under renewed pressure. He said his only remaining bearish puts are on Palantir and MetLife, while emphasizing that he continues evaluating new short opportunities. Approximately 25% of his portfolio is now held in cash, largely from profitable put positions and additional capital. Burry is looking for investment opportunities but refuses to force trades simply to deploy available funds. He stressed that his bullish positioning is temporary and does not necessarily signal that he believes the market has bottomed. The move reflects a significant reduction in his bearish exposure while preserving cash and flexibility to reposition. $PLTR $MET

items.content_excerpt: $ALT $AMD $CELH $SOFI KRKNF ELF NFLX HNST MCRB FUBO These market movements are more a reflection of perception than fundamentals. Perception is 9/10ths of the game in the short term, but eventually fundamentals win out. The question is, who's going to hold through the trough? A lot of folks realized massive capital gains in the first half of the year and I expect many of them to sell their losing positions throughout December to offset those realized gains and reduce their tax liabilities. That could create additional selling pressure, particularly on small and mid-cap names that are already severely beaten down. I see a STRIKING resemblance to '22 in terms of deteriorating sentiment, multiple compression, indiscriminate selling and investors abandoning fundamentally sound companies over macroeconomic uncertainty. Those who were accumulating quality names near the '22 lows made ridiculous amounts of money over the following 12-36 months. Personally, I wouldn't be surprised to see more red throughout the first 3 weeks of December, followed by a bottoming process as year-end tax-loss harvesting subsides and capital gets redeployed heading into '27. I think we could see the beginning of a serious uptrend in Q1. In the meantime, I'm buying up everything I can with the dry powder I've been stashing away specifically for these situations. If the underlying fundamentals and my investment thesis haven't materially changed, why would I not take advantage of these valuations?

items.content_excerpt: $IBRX Agree. A 455% increase in Janus Henderson's IBRX position is difficult to dismiss as random portfolio noise. This doesn't guarantee success, but it is exactly the kind of smart-money behavior long-term investors want to see.

items.title: $IBRX [PART 2 of 2] What about the Nelson Peltz speculation? According to several sources, the $400 million, exercisable through April 15, 2
items.content_excerpt: $IBRX [PART 2 of 2] What about the Nelson Peltz speculation? According to several sources, the $400 million, exercisable through April 15, 2027, subject to conditions, is growth-capital and balance-sheet planning — not the structure normally used to announce or facilitate an imminent acquisition or partnership deal. So why would Janus Henderson (Peltz) dramatically increase its stake in IBRX? It is likely a high-conviction public-equity investment. A straightforward explanation is that the portfolio manager became more confident in ANKTIVA’s commercial momentum. Q3 revenue reached $48.7 million, up 53% from a year earlier, supported by a broader FDA label and the potential to expand into BCG-naïve NMIBC. The purchase may reflect a view that the market is underpricing a transition from development-stage biotech to a growing oncology commercial company. Positioning ahead of catalysts—not necessarily M&A. Just trying to make sense of things. Other ideas are welcomed.

items.title: $IBRX — [PART 1 of 2] IMO, the recent financing disclosure signals a more of a positive than negative outlook. The company had already repor
items.content_excerpt: $IBRX — [PART 1 of 2] IMO, the recent financing disclosure signals a more of a positive than negative outlook. The company had already reported more than $350 million of cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities (June 30), alongside rapidly growing product revenue. The amendment is therefore consistent with funding commercialization, manufacturing/supply, and clinical/regulatory expansion from a position of greater negotiating leverage. So, when it arranged additional financing, it likely was not doing so because it was desperate for money. It can use the funding to: • Hire sales and support staff to expand ANKTIVA’s launch (e.g., recent Dunkirk job listings). • Make or secure enough drug supply for more patients and markets • Pay for clinical trials and regulatory submissions for new uses or countries The November 23 disclosure points more strongly to ImmunityBio preparing to operate independently than to it signaling a near-term partnership or sale.

items.title: @BosqueBandit A $PDSB Big Pharma deal for PDS0301 is likely a post-Phase 2b story. Management pivoted all-in on mCRC in August, and while th
items.content_excerpt: @BosqueBandit A $PDSB Big Pharma deal for PDS0301 is likely a post-Phase 2b story. Management pivoted all-in on mCRC in August, and while the NCI Phase 2 data is strong, BP rarely pays up before randomized Phase 2b data de-risks it, especially with up to $116M in milestones and a 10% royalty owed to Merck KGaA. Patrick Soon-Shiong’s Nant Capital led the $22.3M PIPE for this pivot, and PDS0301’s IL-12 mechanism pairs well with $IBRX’s Anktiva, though $IBRX has its own cash burn priorities. Meanwhile, NantWorks holds a 1-year exclusive window to license shelved Phase 3-ready PDS0101. Odds of a deal look moderate given strong JAMA-published HNSCC survival data and fresh patents, but because PDSB won't self-fund it, NantWorks holds the leverage. Expect a JV or back-end milestone deal rather than a huge upfront check. The drugs for each company are stellar, my issue is how insiders reap the financial rewards through warrants, options and grants while diluting retail into oblivion.

items.content_excerpt: $IONQ @VectorAtomic, an IonQ company, has been awarded the Phase II Option of their Gravimeter using Rubidium Atoms with Vibration-immunity for the Maritime and Airborne Platforms (GRAVMAP) program from the @DARPA. GRAVMAP will produce the first strapdown quantum gravimeter to operate on an airborne platform, with program work focusing on the improvement of size, weight, and power (SWaP); ability to operate throughout representative dynamics; and manufacturability of the company’s existing gravimetry technologies. Originally awarded in September 2025, the program’s latest achievement was vibration analysis of the newly designed top-level assembly. Complete system integration and laboratory evaluation of the sensor’s performance will occur throughout the remainder of 2026, with field testing and platform demonstrations slated for 2027.

$APLD: What Changed in Today’s November Investor presentation from $APLD $APLD’s November investor presentation shows more signed business, stronger lease economics, construction progress and clearer campus locations. This comparison uses the June 2026 corporate deck, the latest earlier full presentation I could verify. Against June, $APLD’s signed capacity increased 10.6% to 1,560 MW; base-term lease value rises 15.1%, from $35.73 billion to $41.13 billion; and value including all renewals reaches $98.36 billion from $85.66 billion. The new 150 MW lease supplies the $5.4 billion increase. The $98.36 billion includes base terms and assumes all renewals occur. The $41.13 billion represents expected rent over 15 to 18 years, subject to delivery and contractual conditions; neither figure is today’s asset value. Clearer locations for Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 2 June left the locations of PF3 and DF2 undisclosed. No more. November’s campus table now identifies Polaris Forge 3 in Center, North Dakota, and Delta Forge 2 in Alabama. ￼I know that location is in Brookwood. These are the existing 300 MW PF3 project and 210 MW DF2 project, respectively. The presentation gives shareholders a more concrete picture of the $APLD portfolio across North Dakota, Louisiana and Alabama. For PF3, naming Center, ND as the location helps connect the campus with the Base Electron generation project described in $APLD’s October 10-Q. Naming Alabama gives investors a clearer jurisdiction for following DF2’s power and permitting developments, although its city remains unspecified in the deck. But that city is Brookwood. The new lease deserves a closer look The new lease agreement covers 150 MW for 18 years, with three five-year renewal options. It carries $5.4 billion of expected base rent, approximately $12.7 billion with all renewals, an expected 85% site NOI margin and planned deliveries during 2028. The location of this separate 150 MW lease remains undisclosed. Dividing $5.4 billion by 18 years produces $300 million of average annual rent, or $2 million per MW. PF3 and DF1 each produce approximately $1.67 million per MW using the same calculation. That puts the new contract about 20% higher on average annual rent per MW, consistent with $APLD management’s statement that pricing improved. Its larger value reflects both a longer term and better average economics. This calculation does not establish a 20% increase in starting rent because the escalation schedules and project differences are not disclosed. At the assumed 85% margin, the new lease contributes approximately $255 million of average annual site NOI. Against projected construction costs of $11 million to $13 million per MW, that equals roughly 13.1% to 15.5% of development cost annually before financing and corporate costs. The Enlarged $2.30 billion NOI figure is useful, with a specific meaning The June investor presentation described approximately $2 billion of average annualized NOI. The November presentation provides a site-by-site model totaling approximately $2.30 billion, with a $2.22 billion to $2.38 billion range. The model divides each lease’s base-term value by its duration, applies the expected operating margin and assumes all capacity operates and bills for a full year. The strongest execution evidence In the November Investor Presentation is the operating capacity $APLD’s operating AI capacity rises from 100 MW in June to 275 MW in the updated deck. $APLD’s November 24 announcement explains the latest milestone: PF1 has 250 MW operational, and PF2’s first 25 MW data hall achieved Ready for Service on schedule. Base-build commissioning also finished for the first 75 MW at PF2, with the remaining 50 MW still requiring fit-out and customer delivery. $APLD achieving ready for service at a second campus provides evidence that $APLD can repeat its construction and commissioning process. That is execution. However, only about 18% of the 1,560 MW signed portfolio is online. According to several sources, the $400 million, exercisable through April 15, 2027, subject to conditions, is growth-capital and balance-sheet planning — not the structure normally used to announce or facilitate an imminent acquisition or partnership deal. So why would Janus Henderson (Peltz) dramatically increase its stake in IBRX? It is likely a high-conviction public-equity investment. A straightforward explanation is that the portfolio manager became more confident in ANKTIVA’s commercial momentum. Q3 revenue reached $48.7 million, up 53% from a year earlier, supported by a broader FDA label and the potential to expand into BCG-naïve NMIBC. The purchase may reflect a view that the market is underpricing a transition from development-stage biotech to a growing oncology commercial company. Positioning ahead of catalysts—not necessarily M&A. Just trying to make sense of things. Other ideas are welcomed.

$IBRX — [PART 1 of 2] IMO, the recent financing disclosure signals a more of a positive than negative outlook. The company had already reported more than $350 million of cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities (June 30), alongside rapidly growing product revenue. The amendment is therefore consistent with funding commercialization, manufacturing/supply, and clinical/regulatory expansion from a position of greater negotiating leverage. So, when it arranged additional financing, it likely was not doing so because it was desperate for money. It can use the funding to: • Hire sales and support staff to expand ANKTIVA’s launch (e.g., recent Dunkirk job listings). • Make or secure enough drug supply for more patients and markets • Pay for clinical trials and regulatory submissions for new uses or countries The November 23 disclosure points more strongly to ImmunityBio preparing to operate independently than to it signaling a near-term partnership or sale.
